We reconstruct Tables 8.1–8.6 of Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016), [*Empirical Asset Pricing*](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/empirical-asset-pricing-the-cross-section-of-stock-returns-p-9781118095041).
The sample consists of CRSP common stocks at the end of each month from June 1963 through November 2012.
We use legacy CRSP daily and monthly stock returns and the corresponding Fama–French factors.
See @sec-data-vintages for the source vintages.

## Estimating Beta {#estimate-market-beta}

The CAPM predicts that a stock's expected excess return is its market beta times the market risk premium, $\mathbb E[r_i]=\beta_i\mathbb E[MKT]$.
To estimate beta, regress the stock's historical excess return $r_{i,s}=R_{i,s}-R_{f,s}$ on the market excess return $MKT_s$, with an intercept.
For stock $i$ at the end of month $t$,

$$
r_{i,s}=\alpha_i+\beta_i MKT_s+\varepsilon_{i,s},
\qquad
\widehat\beta_{i,t}
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{s\in W_t}(r_{i,s},MKT_s)}
{\operatorname{Var}_{s\in W_t}(MKT_s)},
$$

where $W_t$ is the estimation window ending in month $t$.
Both moments use the same dates with valid stock and market returns.
BEM use the following windows and minimum observation counts (§8.1).

| Return frequency | Window | Minimum observations |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Daily | 1, 3, 6, 12, or 24 months | 15, 50, 100, 200, or 450 |
| Monthly | 1, 2, 3, or 5 years | 10, 20, 24, or 24 |

Suppose a stock trades infrequently.
Its return may reflect news that first moved the market on a different trading day.
BEM consider two adjustments that use a year of daily returns and a 200-observation minimum.
Scholes–Williams uses three separate slopes $b_{-1}$, $b_0$, and $b_{+1}$ from regressing $r_{i,s}$ on $MKT_{s+k}$ one at a time.
Dimson uses the slopes $\gamma_k$ from one regression with all eleven market returns from $s-5$ through $s+5$ as predictors.

$$
\widehat\beta^{SW}_{i,t}
=\frac{\widehat b_{-1}+\widehat b_0+\widehat b_{+1}}{1+2\widehat\rho_M},
\qquad
\widehat\beta^{D}_{i,t}=\sum_{k=-5}^{5}\widehat\gamma_k,
$$

where $\widehat\rho_M$ is the market return's first-order autocorrelation over the estimation window.
We shift the market series on the trading calendar before joining it to stock returns.
A lag can precede the first stock-return date in the window.
We omit response dates whose market lead falls after formation and apply the minimum to the remaining complete observations.
This keeps all beta inputs observable at formation.
